evidence.note: Opening plan is a coarse ordered sequence: explore env → read existing skeleton → update requirements/install → write app (core setup, storage, auth, idempotency, then routes, then workers). Rough decomposition exists but it's a single monolithic-write plan, not a milestone hierarchy with per-item done-conditions.
Verification deliberately begins with boot+auth first — health endpoint then auth 401 checks — establishing a bootable authed skeleton as the earliest verified milestone.

The three named traps are recognized as distinct workstreams and each gets an explicit concrete done-condition during testing: PI state machine (capture/cancel on succeeded → payment_intent_unexpected_state), idempotency (same key+body replay, different body → 400 idempotency_error, error replay), and webhook endpoints CRUD — and these risky checks were run ahead of finishing remaining CRUD breadth.

Sequencing is partly reactive rather than a pre-committed milestone plan: remaining CRUD (products/prices/subscriptions/refunds/restricted keys) tested after traps, bugs discovered mid-stream (decline status, card-lookup, confirm:true) triggering a full rewrite — showing the traps were bundled into one big build rather than ring-fenced as first-class incremental milestones.

reasoning: The agent clearly ordered work as boot+auth → core CRUD → the trap subsystems, and treated the PI state machine, idempotency, and webhooks as distinct workstreams each verified with concrete done-conditions, which exceeds the flat-checklist level (3) and satisfies the level-5 milestone/trap-recognition description. It edges toward 8 because the risky subsystems got explicit checks front-loaded ahead of finishing the CRUD breadth, but falls short of 8/10 because the build was a single monolithic write rather than ring-fenced first-class milestones, the plans were largely tactical/step-by-step and reactive, and there was no explicit up-front dependency map or acceptance-condition-per-milestone structure.
